newsitem.title: INDIA: India says to speed up cargo clearance at ports.
newsitem.headline: India says to speed up cargo clearance at ports.

text.p: India said on Thursday it was taking steps to speed up cargo clearance at all major ports and cut the waiting time for loading and unloading of ships.

"All major ports have been asked to launch a three-month campaign starting from September 1 for preventing pre-berthing delays and with a view to ensure that no ship has to wait for berthing for more than 24 hours," Surface Transport Minister T.G. Venkatraman told reporters.
Yogendra Narain, the highest ranking civil servant in the Surface Transport Ministry, said: "Our idea is that pre-berthing delay is reduced so that demurrage cost is reduced."
Venkatraman denied reports that foreign companies were shying away from investing in India because of port congestion.
"There is no truth in the fact that major companies are shying away due to port congestion."
Venkatraman said his ministry had authorised the heads of all 11 major ports in India to replace officials found lagging in speeding up berthing services.
Narain said the government has also decided not to subject coastal ships to customs checks and clearance as this delayed shipping operations. "A notification to that effect will be issued soon."
Coastal shipping is reserved for Indian ships that sail from one Indian port to another. They had been subjected to customs checks, which shippers say are cumbersome and unwarranted.
But removing the checks means ports will have to segregate domestic cargoes from foreign ones, which are still subjected to inspections, a ministry official said.
Narain said Indian ports handled 227 million tonnes of cargoes in 1996/97 (April-March), compared with 215.5 million tonnes in the previous year.
He said about 180 million tonnes of cargo-handling capacity was expected to be built during the ninth five-year plan (1997-2002), out of which 122 million tonnes would be for the 11 major ports.

"This would require an investment of about 150 billion rupees ($4.2 billion), out of which private sector investment is expected to be about 60 billion," Narain said. "The rest is envisaged from internal resources and budgetary support."
India has 11 major ports and 139 minor ports along its 5,560-km (3,475-mile) coastline that handle about 90 percent of its foreign trade.
Narain said that 22 projects are to be developed by the private sector in line with India's ambitious economic reform programme in 1991, which opened its ports to private and foreign investors.
So far the private sector has decided to develop three projects, he said. "We have invited bids for three more projects," he added.
The three projects opened for bidding are for cargo handling facilities at New Mangalore and Vishakapatman ports and an oil terminal at the Jawaharlal Nehru port near Bombay. ($1 = 35.7 rupees)
